acceptable.choice: An off-the-shelf class booking service (SaaS) configured by the agent, not custom code
acceptable.why: Booking a place in a class with a capacity limit, cancellation and reminder emails is a solved problem: services built for it stop double bookings, the vendor keeps it running, and the owner can change times and prices from a phone, all for less than 30 USD a month.

acceptable.choice: Small-studio class booking tools such as Bookwhen, SimplyBook.me (classes feature), Punchpass, OfferingTree or Momence on its entry or per-booking-fee plan
acceptable.why: They are made for timetabled classes with capacity, client self-cancellation, reminders and class packs, and their entry plans are usually within or close to the budget at 200 clients and 300 classes a month.

acceptable.choice: General scheduling tools with group or class events, such as Acuity Scheduling (Squarespace Scheduling), Square Appointments, Setmore or Zoho Bookings
acceptable.why: Cheap or free tiers cover group sessions with capacity limits, email reminders and an easy admin app, which is enough if the studio doesn't need memberships or complex packs.
It works for simple capacity-limited classes on a paid plan, but it is weak at recurring timetables, class packs and studio-style client accounts, so it is a fallback, not the first choice.

acceptable.choice: Embedding the service's booking widget or link in an existing website, social profile or a simple hosted site (for example Squarespace or Wix)
acceptable.why: Clients get one obvious place to see the timetable and book, and there is still no server for anyone to look after.

ruled_out.choice: A custom-built web app (for example Next.js, Django or Rails with a database) written and hosted by the agent
ruled_out.why: The owner can't debug, read logs or edit code, so every outage, security patch or change depends on paying for help. That breaks 'it not breaking' and 'change it myself', and it rebuilds something cheap services already do.

ruled_out.choice: A self-managed VPS or server (DigitalOcean, EC2, etc.)
ruled_out.why: The owner wants no server to manage and can't do patching, backups or monitoring.

ruled_out.choice: Keeping the spreadsheet as the booking system (Google Forms or Apps Script writing to Sheets)
ruled_out.why: Nothing stops two people booking the last place at once, so the double booking it is meant to fix carries on, and when scripts fail they fail silently where the owner can't see.

ruled_out.choice: No-code app builders on top of Airtable or Sheets (Glide, Softr, Bubble, Zapier chains)
ruled_out.why: Capacity checks, cancellations and reminders have to be hand-built from fragile parts that a non-technical owner can't fix when an automation or API limit breaks.

ruled_out.choice: A WordPress site with a booking plugin (Amelia, Bookly) on self-chosen hosting
ruled_out.why: Plugin, theme and PHP updates, plus security, are ongoing maintenance the owner can't do.

ruled_out.choice: Enterprise studio platforms such as Mindbody, Glofox, WellnessLiving, Mariana Tek or ClassPass-style suites
ruled_out.why: Typical pricing is roughly 100 to 400 USD or more a month, well over the 30 USD budget, and far more than a single small studio needs.

must_mention: The honest recommendation is not to build software: subscribe to an existing class booking service, and have the agent set it up rather than write code.
Capacity limits enforced by the system, so a place can't be booked twice, are what fix the double booking problem.
The owner should open and own the account in their own name, with their own login and billing, so they aren't dependent on the agent or anyone else.
The owner changes class times and prices in the service's admin screen or phone app, and the agent should write short step-by-step instructions for these common tasks.

Check the chosen plan covers the essentials: a recurring timetable, a capacity per class, client booking and cancellation (ideally with a cancellation cut-off), automatic reminder emails, and a mobile-friendly booking page.
Costs: the monthly fee, and if payments are taken online, card processing fees (usually about 2 to 3 percent per transaction) or a per-booking fee on top, checked against the 30 USD limit.
Use the free trial and test with a few real clients before switching everyone over.

A switch-over plan: import or invite the 200 clients from the spreadsheet, run the old and new systems side by side briefly, then stop email and spreadsheet bookings so there is only one source of truth.

Client data and privacy: the service holds client personal data, so its privacy and data-protection terms (GDPR or the local equivalent) matter, and there should be a way to export clients and bookings.
The agent should say clearly what it can do (compare options, configure, migrate, write guides) and what it can't (it doesn't run in the background, so support comes from the vendor).
red_flags: Recommending a custom-coded app, a database or a server for this owner, or presenting the agent as the ongoing maintainer of custom infrastructure.
Proposing Google Sheets or Forms with scripts as the booking engine, which keeps the double-booking risk and adds silent failures.
Recommending Mindbody or a similar enterprise platform without saying it costs several times the budget.
Quoting exact prices or feature availability as certain without telling the owner to check current pricing, since plans and tiers change often.
Ignoring payment processing fees or per-booking commissions when claiming the cost is under budget.
Setting up accounts under the agent's own or a third party's control, or anything that locks the owner out of their own data.
Having the agent handle or store card details directly instead of using the platform's built-in payment provider (Stripe, Square, PayPal).
Instructions that assume technical skill (DNS, API keys, webhooks, editing code) for jobs the owner will have to do themselves.
Recommending a fragile chain of integrations (Zapier or Make linking several tools) as the core booking flow.
unknowns: Whether clients pay online when booking, pay at the studio, or use class packs or memberships, which decides which tools and plans fit.
Country and currency, which affect available payment providers, pricing, tax and data-protection rules.
Whether the studio already has a website or domain the booking page should sit in.
How many teachers or rooms there are, and whether teachers need their own logins.
The cancellation policy and waitlist needs, such as late-cancel cut-offs, fees and automatically filling freed places from a waitlist.
Whether SMS reminders are wanted on top of email, which is often a paid add-on.
The exact current price and plan limits of each candidate service at this size, which need checking on vendor sites or during a free trial.
How the owner likes to work, such as phone app or desktop, and how comfortable they are with an admin dashboard, which is best judged in a trial.
